Instead they hand you a python simulation of a token/vault system with a vulnerability planted and you audit it live, talking through your process while the interviewer probes. The bug classes they apparently pull from: a reentrancy analog where withdraw() invokes a user-supplied hook/callback BEFORE decrementing the balance (checks-effects-interactions violated), integer truncation in fee math where rounding always favors the user, and share-price inflation on the first depositor of a vault. I want exactly that as a practice round: a repo where the code looks clean, exactly one test fails, and the fix is a small reordering or a rounding direction change. 60 minutes, interviewer pressure on. If you can make the planted bug the checks-effects-interactions ordering one specifically, even better, thats the one i keep missing in CTFs.
stress_rationale: The user prescribes the exact vulnerability class, and the generator must plant a reentrancy analog in synchronous python — a language where reentrancy barely exists — such that exactly one test catches it. EVM/audit vocabulary (checks-effects-interactions, share inflation, rounding direction) stresses the expectation-sentence gates and tempts the generator into untestable security prose.

description: GIS company, web mapping team (esri competitor basically), so the interview is in typescript since thats what the whole front end and their tile server tooling is in. description: Interviewing with a national lab group, computational physics — their life is migrating fortran 77 codes to modern fortran with python bindings and they screen for people who can read numerics and make them fast. They told me the format in advance because its basically a take-home done live: you get a WORKING but deliberately slow python port of a 2D heat diffusion stencil (5-point laplacian, explicit euler stepping, halo/ghost cells around the boundary), all tests already passing, and the task is make it faster WITHOUT changing any numerical results — theyre watching whether you hoist allocations out of the time loop, avoid recomputing the halo every step, maybe restructure the update sweep, that kind of thing. So the starting repo should have zero failing tests and the deliverable is essentially the diff plus my explanation. Is that a shape zenkai supports? Tests green before, tests green after, the change itself is what gets judged. 90 minutes, no interviewer for the first hour then they join to review my diff.

description: So this is a weird one. Big insurance company, "actuarial transformation" team, which translated from corporate speak means: two decades of SAS programs that price and reserve everything, and they are converting it all to python. The OA is 2 parts, 75 minutes total, no human on the call, webcam proctored. Part 1 per the prep sheet: they show you a SAS data step — with RETAIN across rows, BY-group processing with FIRST.var and LAST.var flags, the implicit loop over observations — and you reimplement the same logic in python. plain python, i asked if pandas is allowed and the coordinator didnt know, so assume no, dicts and lists. If youve never read SAS, RETAIN means a variable keeps its value across iterations instead of resetting, and FIRST./LAST. are true on the first/last row of each by-group, its how everyone does grouped running totals. Part 2 is actuarial-flavored: a loss reserving triangle, compute chain-ladder age-to-age development factors and project the ultimate losses, they give the triangle as rows of paid amounts by accident year and development period. I took exam P years ago and remember roughly none of it, but the math itself is just weighted ratios and cumulative products, its the off by one on development periods thatll kill me. Can zenkai generate this as a two part timed OA? Deadpan corporate tone in the problem statements would honestly be good practice for the real thing.
stress_rationale: SAS data-step semantics (RETAIN, FIRST./LAST. by-group flags, the implicit row loop) and chain-ladder reserving are about as far from LC distribution as it gets — both parts are pure invention that must independently clear every validator gate, and the expectation sentences must faithfully carry actuarial/SAS vocabulary without collapsing into generic array-problem phrasing.

description: Long shot but here goes. I've been an automation tech at a municipal water treatment plant for 6 years — ladder logic, Allen-Bradley PLCs, wonderware HMI screens, the whole IEC 61131 world — and im interviewing for a "controls software engineer" job at a company that builds SCADA supervisory software in python, so like one level up from the PLCs. What im told is the exercise simulates the kind of logic i already know cold from ladder: a state machine for a pump sequence with interlocks and timers. In my world its all TON timers (on-delay, output goes true after the input has been true for the preset time), debounce on float switches because they chatter, permissives and interlocks (chlorine pump must NOT run unless the flow switch has proven flow for 5 seconds, that kind of thing), fail-safe on loss of signal. The horror stories in this industry are all interlock bugs — a pump that keeps injecting chlorine after flow stopped because someone latched a bit and never unlatched it. Anyway what i want from zenkai: a python round that simulates a small pump/chemical-feed controller with a planted interlock or timer bug and one failing test that exposes it, and me having to find it while the interviewer asks questions, because thats the format. Two important things. One, the time stuff cant be real sleeps right? in ladder the scan cycle is the clock — i assume the python version should take time as an input i can step, otherwise the tests would take forever and be flaky. Two, please keep the repo SMALL, like 3 source files max — im not a software engineer yet, when i opened a friends practice repo with 14 files i just shut the laptop. 60 minutes. Sorry for the wall of text, day shift was long.
stress_rationale: A long noisy brief with the two load-bearing requirements buried near the end (injectable stepped clock instead of real sleeps; a hard 3-source-file cap) — exactly the extraction test a rambling real user poses. TON-timer and interlock semantics from ladder logic must become deterministic clock-injected python, and the file cap collides with the generator's tendency to sprawl simulation scaffolding.
